originalGroup.material:
A night train without a destination

The first thing to say about my grandfather's model railway (0) IS that it does not represent an actual place. Visitors nevertheless spend several minutes trying to identify the town, as ____1____ every miniature station must have a real counterpart. He enjoys their guesses but never confirms one.

What appeals to him is not so ____2____ the machinery as the possibility of inventing a landscape. A hill can be moved, a tunnel extended and a whole street redesigned before the next train arrives. None of this depends ____3____ the geography of the district outside his window.

For years, he would allow nobody else to touch the layout. Then his granddaughter asked to build a café beside the station. At first he was on the ____4____ of refusing: the proposed building was much brighter than anything already there. Instead, he handed her a piece of card.

The café is now the busiest-looking building in the town, complete with customers whose coats she painted individually. Far ____5____ spoiling the model, her contribution gave him ideas for other changes. He has even left a space for a building that she has yet ____6____ design.

There is no question ____7____ turning the railway into a precise historical reconstruction. That would defeat its purpose. As he puts it, the pleasure lies in making room for what might have been, ____8____ than proving what once existed.

originalGroup.material:
The menu between two languages

Translating a restaurant menu (0) IS often described as a matter of replacing one set of food names with another. Anyone who has tried it knows there is more ____1____ it than that. A name may tell local diners how a dish is prepared while giving a visitor no useful clue at all.

The translator has to decide ____2____ to retain the unfamiliar name or replace it with a description. Neither choice is automatically superior. Keeping the name may preserve a connection with local practice; a brief explanation can tell diners what they will actually receive.

Problems arise when an attractive phrase is used at the ____3____ of accuracy. Calling something a cake, for example, may create expectations that its texture does not fulfil. The translation can sound perfectly natural and still fail to give a fair impression ____4____ the dish.

One café owner therefore invited the translator into the kitchen. Only ____5____ did she discover that a word she had understood as a cooking method was the family name of a former owner. The recipe itself had changed several times.

They revised the menu together, taking account ____6____ what diners needed to know as well as what the café wished to celebrate. Some names remained, followed by short explanations. Others were replaced. The result was neither a dictionary ____7____ a collection of decorative stories. It was a practical text whose success depended ____8____ helping people make choices at a table.

originalGroup.material:
The path nobody planned

The narrow track across our campus (0) IS absent from the original plans. It appeared gradually as students cut across the grass on their way to the library. By the time the grounds team noticed it, the route had already come ____1____ regular use.

A notice asked people to keep to the paved paths, but it had little ____2____ on their behaviour. The unofficial track connected two busy entrances directly, whereas the planned route involved three corners. People had not invented the shortcut merely for the ____3____ of damaging a lawn.

The obvious response seemed to be paving the track. Yet that raised a question: what ____4____ another convenient route appeared next month? The team could not simply turn every line of worn grass into a permanent path without considering drainage and access.

Instead of deciding on the ____5____ of a single photograph, they watched how the area was used over several weeks. They found that some people took the shortcut only when late for a particular lecture; others used it throughout the day. The distinction helped explain why the grass wore unevenly.

Eventually, a new path was built along part of the route, with its position adjusted to leave enough space ____6____ rainwater to drain. The decision did not establish a rule that every shortcut should be followed. It did show the value of finding ____7____ why a route exists before removing or formalising it. A design can be improved by attending to use, provided that use is not mistaken ____8____ the only consideration.

originalGroup.material:
The laugh beyond the microphone

A recording of an interview (0) IS never quite the same experience as being present in the room. Microphones capture sound, but a listener may have no idea ____1____ a speaker is pointing to. Even a perfectly audible sentence can depend on something beyond the recording.

During an oral-history project, one interviewer discovered this ____2____ accident. A guest said, "That was the one," and everyone laughed. Months later, nobody listening to the file could tell which photograph the guest had picked up or why it was amusing.

The team had taken care to obtain permission, check the equipment and label the files. What they had failed to take ____3____ account was how frequently people communicate by looking, pointing or sharing a memory without naming it. The missing information could not be restored merely by turning ____4____ the volume.

In later sessions, interviewers sometimes asked a speaker to describe the object being discussed. They did so without interrupting every gesture, since too much explanation could prevent the conversation ____5____ developing naturally. A short note after the interview was occasionally more appropriate.

There was no guarantee that every later question would be answered. The aim was to make the record usable to someone other ____6____ the people who had been there. That required attention to the circumstances in ____7____ the words were spoken, as well as to the words themselves. The laughter was worth keeping, even if its cause could never be explained ____8____ full.
